title: Large deviations in quantum dynamics and complexity
abstract: We study three definitions of large deviation in many-body quantum dynamics: (i) via the full distribution of an extensive observable, (ii) via the distribution of measurement outcomes (from a continuous monitoring of the observable) over a time interval $t \le t_{\max}$, and (iii) via the distribution of expectation values over $t \le t_{\max}$. In generic systems without conservation laws, the large deviation function (i) reaches its longtime limit at $t \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$, independently of system size $N$. (ii) and (iii) reach their longtime limit at $t \sim e^{ N}$ and $t \sim \exp(e^{N})$, respectively. Before that, there is a {\it sharp} frontier between the explored and unexplored outcomes/expectation values; their distribution equals the longtime limit truncated at values that drift with $t_{\max}$. We propose that the evolution of these values with $t_{\max}$ provides a measure of quantum complexity.
summary: This paper develops a theory linking large deviation functions in quantum dynamics to a measure of quantum complexity. By comparing three definitions—full distribution, measurement outcomes, and expectation values—the authors find that while some quantities equilibrate rapidly, others exhibit extremely slow saturation times ($\exp(e^N)$). This time dependence is proposed as the quantitative signature of complex quantum evolution.
main_problem: The study investigates how different definitions of large deviations manifest in many-body quantum dynamics, proposing that their time evolution provides a measure of quantum complexity.
main_result: While the full distribution equilibrates quickly ($t \sim O(1)$), distributions derived from continuous monitoring or expectation values exhibit much slower saturation times ($	ext{t}_{\max} \sim e^N$ or $\exp(e^N)$), which is proposed as a complexity measure.
method: The authors employ large deviation theory, analyzing generating functions for observables and mapping the long-time behavior onto equilibrium statistical mechanics models (like Mattis models).
model_or_system: The analysis uses the kicked Ising model as a primary example system. The dynamics are analyzed in the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$) by relating quantum expectation values to classical spin systems on a torus.
key_observables: Full distribution of extensive observables, outcome distributions from continuous monitoring, and expectation value distributions ($\langle A angle_t$).
important_parameters: System size $N$, time $	ext{t}_{\max}$, and the characteristic scales $O(1)$, $e^N$, and $\exp(e^N)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on mapping quantum dynamics to classical statistical ensembles (like the XY model) in the long-time limit, and assumes certain thermalization properties.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of rescaled generating functions at $t \sim O(1)$ for the full distribution, while other figures show time evolution plots comparing measured distributions to predictions from Mattis models or binomial statistics.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares three definitions of large deviations. It first shows rapid equilibration for the full observable distribution. Subsequently, it analyzes continuous monitoring and expectation values, deriving distinct, much slower saturation timescales that are interpreted as measures of quantum complexity.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework to quantify 'quantum complexity' not through entanglement entropy alone, but by analyzing the time scales required for rare fluctuations in observables to saturate their limiting distributions.
